caseLines.text: If you trust Prescott to hold his QB4 pace, this fills your empty QB slot and sells a WR whose usage is fading. The other manager is out of the race and gets a WR for a thin lineup, so he should say yes. The cost is a short second flex slot.

If you are fine with one TE, this gets you a locked-in QB for a push. The other manager is out of the race and gets the better TE, so he should take it. The playbook rates QBs and TEs the lowest, so this costs you little.
If you want a top QB now and believe Flowers keeps cooling off, this is worth it. You fix your empty QB slot with the best QB on the list. Dak Picks is out of the race and gets a WR it needs.
If you trust Mahomes to stay a top QB on a strong offense, this is a fair swap. You fill your QB need and the other manager gets a WR for the stretch run. It costs you WR depth.

If you want a real QB1 and can live with one startable tight end, this is worth sending. You fill your biggest weak slot and keep your RB and WR depth. The other manager is out of the race and gets the bigger name in McBride.

If you want a QB1 and can live with a thinner WR group, this swap gets you one. The other manager is out of the race and gets a WR who lines up with the roster, so it should say yes. Flowers is slumping, so you give up a cooling player.

If you trust Prescott to keep scoring, this trade is worth it, because you go from no usable QB to a top QB. You still keep one TE after giving up McBride. The other manager is out of the race and gets the better player.
If you believe Flowers keeps slumping, selling him for Prescott is a fair gut call, as long as you can patch FLEX2. You fix QB and the other manager gets the better player.

If you want your empty QB slot filled by a top QB, this is worth it, since you give up a TE you can live without. Prescott is hot and on a strong offense, and the other manager is out of the race and gets the better player.
